properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 9 at 12:59PM MST until October 12 at 5:00AM MST by NWS Flagstaff AZ
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible.

* WHERE...Yavapai, western Coconino, northern Gila, and far southern
Navajo counties.

* WHEN...From Saturday morning through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry
washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas. Low-water
crossings may be flooded.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- A upper-level trough will help pull moisture from the remnants of
Tropical Storm Rachel up into western Arizona to produce showers
and thunderstorms Saturday, followed by extended periods of
rainfall through at least Sunday. Thunderstorms will have the
potential to produce heavy rainfall that could lead to flash
flooding, while extended periods of rain can lead to elevated
streams, rivers, and flow through washes. Greatest risk of heavy
rainfall looks be along higher terrain due to upsloping.
- Additional information is available at weather.gov/flagstaff.
properties.instruction:
Have a way to receive Flash Flood Warnings and be prepared to take
action should warnings be issued.

properties.headline: Air Quality Alert issued October 9 at 2:57PM CDT by NWS Norman OK
properties.description:
The following statement was issued by the Oklahoma Department of
Environmental Quality from 10 AM to 10 PM CDT Saturday.

An Air Quality Alert for Ozone has been issued for Saturday, October
10th, for the Lawton area due to expected high concentrations of
ozone.

Public Health Recommendations: Persons with existing heart or
respiratory ailments should reduce physical exertion and outdoor
activity.

The general public is encouraged to help alleviate the problem by
reducing vehicle miles traveled by riding the bus, carpooling, or
avoiding unnecessary trips. The public is also asked to avoid
refueling during the morning and early afternoon hours, and to avoid
the use of two cycle engines such as lawn mowers, motorcycles, weed
trimmers, and outboard engines. It is also advised to limit outdoor
burning.

To view the latest air quality map, visit airnow.gov or the AirNow
app.

For hourly updates on concentrations and possible health warnings,
telephone the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality at
405-702-4100. For more information on health effects, call the
American Lung Association of Oklahoma at 405-748-4674
properties.note: Non-Weather Emergency Message. Not sent to IPAWS.

properties.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued October 9 at 12:44PM PDT until October 9 at 8:00PM PDT by NWS Phoenix AZ
properties.description:
* WHAT...For the Extreme Heat Warning, dangerously hot conditions.
Afternoon temperatures 104 to 109. Major Heat Risk. Overexposure
can cause heat cramps and heat exhaustion to develop and, without
intervention, can lead to heat stroke. For the Wind Advisory, south
winds 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 50 mph expected.

* WHERE...Imperial County West and Imperial Valley.

* WHEN...For the Extreme Heat Warning, until 8 PM PDT this evening.
For the Wind Advisory, from 2 AM to 5 PM PDT Sunday.

* IMPACTS...Difficult driving conditions, especially for larger
vehicles traveling along roads with crosswinds. Light, unsecured
objects may become airborne. Heat related illnesses increase
significantly during extreme heat events.
properties.instruction:
A Wind Advisory means that sustained wind speeds of between 30 and 40
mph are expected, or wind gusts of between 40 and 58 mph. Winds this
strong can make driving difficult, especially for high profile
vehicles.

In addition, strong winds over desert areas could result in briefly
lowered visibilities to well under a mile at times in blowing dust or
blowing sand. Use extra caution.

An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.

Afternoon temperatures 103 to 105. Major Heat Risk. Overexposure
can cause heat cramps and heat exhaustion to develop and, without
intervention, can lead to heat stroke. For the Wind Advisory, south
winds 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 50 mph expected.

* WHERE...Yuma.

* WHEN...For the Extreme Heat Warning, until 8 PM MST this evening.
For the Wind Advisory, from 2 AM to 5 PM MST Sunday.

* IMPACTS...Difficult driving conditions, especially for larger
vehicles traveling along roads with crosswinds. Light, unsecured
objects may become airborne. Heat related illnesses increase
significantly during extreme heat events.
properties.instruction:
A Wind Advisory means that sustained wind speeds of between 30 and 40
mph are expected, or wind gusts of between 40 and 58 mph. Winds this
strong can make driving difficult, especially for high profile
vehicles.

In addition, strong winds over desert areas could result in briefly
lowered visibilities to well under a mile at times in blowing dust or
blowing sand. Use extra caution.

An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 9 at 12:43PM PDT until October 12 at 5:00AM PDT by NWS Elko NV
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall and debris flows
is possible.

* WHERE...Portions of eastern, northeast, and south central Nevada,
including the following areas, in eastern Nevada, White Pine. In
northeast Nevada, Ruby Mountains and East Humboldt Range in Elko,
South Central Elko and Southeastern Elko. In south central Nevada,
Northeastern Nye and Northwestern Nye.

* WHEN...From Saturday evening through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. In
addition, flash flooding is possible over recently burned areas
like the former Ward Fire, Kearny Fire, Oxley Fire, Secret Pass
Fire, Star Valley Fire, Jones Fire, and Egberts Fire. Other burn
scar locations in the watch area could also be affected.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Deep moisture from decaying Hurricane Rachel is expected to move
northward, crossing into portions of east-central and eastern
Nevada late Saturday night through roughly Monday. This
significant moisture will interact with upper level low pressure
to bring widespread showers with isolated thunderstorms to the
watch area. Moderate to locally heavy rain will cause excessive
runoff and may result in rock, mud, and debris flows in and near
former fire burned areas, steep terrain, and poorly drained urban
areas.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be prepared to take action
should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

properties.areaDesc: Death Valley National Park
properties.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued October 9 at 12:35PM PDT until October 9 at 8:00PM PDT by NWS Las Vegas NV
properties.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with high temperatures near 110
degrees and overnight lows between 80 and 85 degrees. This will
yield at least major Heat Risk, impacting anyone without adequate
cooling and hydration. For the Wind Advisory, south winds 25 to 35
mph with gusts up to 60 mph expected.

* WHERE...Elevations in Death Valley National Park below 2000 feet.

* WHEN...For the Extreme Heat Warning, until 8 PM PDT this evening.
For the Wind Advisory, from 2 PM Saturday to 5 AM PDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Heat-related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events. Gusty winds will blow around unsecured
objects. Tree limbs could be blown down and a few power outages may
result.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...There will likely be a lull in the winds from
late Saturday night through Sunday morning before winds increase
once again Sunday afternoon.
properties.instruction:
Winds this strong can make driving difficult, especially for high
profile vehicles. Use extra caution.

Secure outdoor objects.

Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Monitor the latest forecasts and warnings for updates.

properties.description:
AQAEWX

Atmospheric conditions are expected to be favorable for producing
high levels of ozone air pollution in the Austin area on Saturday.

You can help prevent ozone pollution by sharing a ride, walking
or riding a bicycle, taking your lunch to work, avoiding drive
through lanes, conserving energy, and keeping your vehicle
properly tuned.

If required, the next Ozone Action Day will be issued by 3 PM
on Saturday, October 10, 2026.
